politeq: What is your name? (polite singular here)
repeat: Tu peux répéter, s’il te plaît ?
slow: Tu peux parler plus lentement, s’il te plaît ?
Can you speak more slowly, please? (familiar)
politerepeat: Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ?
Can you repeat, please? (polite singular here)

hello: A daytime greeting usable beyond familiar friends; choose the greeting for the stated situation.
casual: Use this casual greeting in the explicitly familiar-friend role here; it is not a rule for every new acquaintance.
bye: This closes the meeting rather than introducing a new person.
nameq: This is the familiar singular question used in the agreed tu setting. Keep t’ attached to appelles in the written phrase.
Ask for a name in the familiar setting.
politeq: Here vous addresses one person politely. It can also address several people; this scene explicitly has one addressee.
Ask one new adult politely for a name.
alex: Keep m’ with appelle. Alex is an assigned fictional role, not a request for your real name.
camille: Use the assigned name Camille. The phrase does not specify a gender.
andyou: After giving a name, this returns that same question to the familiar conversation partner. The preceding context supplies the topic.
Return the name question to a familiar friend.
andpolite: Return the previous question while keeping the stated polite address.
repeat: Request the words again when you missed them; this does not specifically ask for slower delivery. This composed repair phrase needs fluent confirmation.
Ask a familiar partner for the words again.
slow: Ask for a change of pace when the words are too fast. This is distinct from simply requesting another repetition. This composed phrase needs fluent confirmation.
Ask a familiar partner specifically to slow down.
politerepeat: Use the vous request in the scene that explicitly keeps polite singular address. Exact wording and register need fluent review.
Ask one new adult politely to repeat.
notunderstood: Learn this as a whole repair expression for now; this unit does not assess past-tense conjugation.
Say that you did not understand.
thanks: Thank the person after clarification; this does not supply your name or ask a question.

lessons.title: Greet someone and say goodbye
lessons.goal: Open and close a short meeting in the stated context.
lessons.scenario: Alex meets a familiar friend Camille in the daytime, then leaves.
lessons.usage: Bonjour opens this daytime meeting. Salut is available in the familiar-friend scene; au revoir closes it. More than one greeting can be natural, so tasks specify the intended phrase or exclude equally suitable options.
practice: You arrive during the day. Choose a greeting rather than a farewell or a thank-you.
A familiar friend says hi. Choose the casual greeting shown in the dialogue.
You are leaving the gathering. Say goodbye.
You start a daytime visit with someone new. Choose the general daytime greeting among these options.
At a later meeting, greet a familiar friend casually using the taught phrase.
The visit ends. Close it rather than asking for a name.

lessons.title: Exchange names with a friend
lessons.goal: Give an assigned name, ask a name and return the question.
lessons.scenario: A mutual friend has explicitly invited Alex and Camille to use tu with each other.
lessons.usage: Use the fictional assigned name. Tu and toi belong to this explicitly familiar exchange; they are not universal defaults for every person you meet.
practice: Ask the familiar partner for their name.
You are Camille. Answer the name question.
You are Alex. Answer the returned name question.
You just gave your name. Return that question in this tu conversation.
At another visit you are Alex again. Give that assigned name.
After a brief greeting, ask your familiar partner’s name rather than ending the exchange.

lessons.title: Meet someone politely
lessons.goal: Keep polite singular address through a name exchange.
lessons.scenario: Alex and Camille meet as new adult acquaintances. The exercise explicitly keeps vous.
lessons.usage: The scene specifies polite singular vous. In real interaction, address depends on context and mutual preference; a familiar alternative is not universally wrong.
practice: Ask the new adult’s name while keeping the stated polite vous address.
You are Camille. Supply your assigned name.
Return the name question while keeping polite vous address.
You missed the polite question. Request repetition while retaining vous.
The repeated question asks your name. You are Alex.
At a second formal introduction, ask the name with the stated polite address.

lessons.title: Ask for help understanding
lessons.goal: Signal a missed message, request repetition or a slower pace and acknowledge help.
lessons.scenario: At a lively visit Alex and Camille have agreed to use tu. Read the repair exchange; this draft has no listening assessment.
lessons.usage: Tell the person when you did not understand. Repetition asks for the words again; slower speech asks for a different pace. The task specifies which help is needed.
practice: State that you did not understand; choose the statement rather than a request.
You missed the name under a loud noise. Ask specifically for the words again.
The partner is speaking too fast. Ask specifically for a slower pace.
The clarification helped. Thank your partner.
The clarified question asks your name. You are Alex.
At a later familiar conversation, noise covers a question. Request repetition.

lessons.title: Keep a new exchange going
lessons.goal: Reuse greetings, assigned names and repair in a changed role.
lessons.scenario: At another friend’s home you now play Camille. The partner Alex explicitly agrees to tu.
lessons.usage: Switch the assigned role without switching the learning goal. Ask for clarification when useful. Written choices and reconstruction do not demonstrate listening or spontaneous speaking.
practice: Open the daytime visit with a greeting.
The name question was covered by noise. Ask specifically for repetition.
The question is clear now. You are Camille; give that name.
After your name, return the question to your familiar partner.
Alex speaks too quickly at the next table. Ask specifically for a slower pace.
You leave the visit after introducing yourself. Say goodbye.
